explanations.explanation: Not this time, friend. Saul, Israel's king, gives the order to his son Jonathan and all his servants. But the verse has a twist: “But Jonathan delighted greatly in David,” (1 Samuel 19:1). Delighted people don't usually sign up for that kind of assignment.

That's right. Jonathan, Saul's son, hears the order and delights greatly in David anyway. He doesn't go along with it. He goes and warns David (1 Samuel 19:2). Picture your boss handing you a job and you walking straight to the person it's about to say, "Heads up."

explanations.answer: Find a secret place and hide
explanations.explanation: Yes! Jonathan tells David, “…find a secret place and hide there.” (1 Samuel 19:2). Short, clear instructions with no extra steps. He's got a plan for the field too, so David isn't hiding alone.
Jonathan never says that. His words are to be on guard in the morning, find a secret place and hide there (1 Samuel 19:2). Nobody handed David a suitcase in this verse. Just a hiding spot.

No soldiers in this one, friend. Jonathan's advice is to be on guard in the morning and hide (1 Samuel 19:2). When the king is the problem, a quiet corner beats a whole army marching around. I think that's why this plan is so small and so careful.

You got it, baker. Jonathan says, “He took his life in his hands when he struck down the Philistine, and the LORD worked a great salvation for all Israel.” (1 Samuel 19:5). He's pointing at something Saul watched with his own eyes. That's a strong way to argue with a king.

Jonathan doesn't bring himself into it. He talks about what David did for the king and for all Israel. He reminds Saul that David “took his life in his hands when he struck down the Philistine” (1 Samuel 19:5). It's a case made for his father, not for himself.

Money never comes up, friend. Jonathan's whole point is that David struck down the Philistine, and the LORD worked a great salvation for all Israel (1 Samuel 19:5). That's a much bigger deposit than any bill. Not an accounting department in sight.
That's it. Jonathan tells his father, “You saw it and rejoiced” (1 Samuel 19:5). Think about how that lands. Jonathan is basically saying, "Dad, you were there, and you were glad."
Jonathan says something different. His words are, “You saw it and rejoiced” (1 Samuel 19:5). Saul wasn't a quiet bystander in Jonathan's telling. He was glad about what happened.

The verse doesn't mention tears. It says Saul saw it and rejoiced (1 Samuel 19:5). Maybe there was some emotion in the room, but I'm only going on what Jonathan actually says. Rejoicing is the word he picks.

Yes, innocent. Jonathan asks, “…why would you sin against innocent blood by killing David for no reason?” (1 Samuel 19:5). Two phrases, one point: David hasn't done anything to deserve this. Jonathan says it right to his father's face.

Close to the palace, but not the word. Jonathan calls it “innocent blood” (1 Samuel 19:5). In the same breath he calls David the king's servant, and he says David has not sinned against him (1 Samuel 19:4). The point is that David did nothing wrong, not who his family is.

That word fits the Philistines, but not David. Jonathan says Saul would be sinning “against innocent blood” (1 Samuel 19:5). David is a servant of the king, not an outsider. Jonathan wants his father to see that nothing David did calls for this.

explanations.answer: Swears an oath to spare David
explanations.explanation: That's right. Saul swears, “As surely as the LORD lives, David will not be put to death.” (1 Samuel 19:6). That's a big promise from the same man who just gave the opposite order. Jonathan's words got through.
Nothing like that happens. The text says Saul “listened to the voice of Jonathan” (1 Samuel 19:6). A king who is listening to you is not reaching for the lock. He swears an oath instead.

No trip to Moab here. Saul swears that David will not be put to death (1 Samuel 19:6). Then Jonathan brings David to Saul, and David is with him as before (1 Samuel 19:7). David stays right where he was.
Yes. Jonathan summons David, tells him everything, and brings him to Saul, and “David was with Saul as before.” (1 Samuel 19:7). Same king, same room, same everything. I bet that felt a little tense.
It's actually true. Jonathan brings David to Saul, and “David was with Saul as before.” (1 Samuel 19:7). For that moment, nothing has changed. David is back at the king's side.

That's the word. David struck the Philistines “with such a mighty blow that they fled before him.” (1 Samuel 19:8). The whole army turned around and ran. Imagine opening the door to a game and the other team is already sprinting for the parking lot.
No bowing from the Philistines. They “fled before him” (1 Samuel 19:8). They were headed away from David, not toward him. Nobody stopped to take a bow.
They did the opposite of gathering. The verse says David struck them with such a mighty blow that they fled before him (1 Samuel 19:8). They ran the other way. David's blow cleared the field.

Yes, and this part is heavy. Saul “tried to pin him to the wall with his spear.” (1 Samuel 19:10). David is just playing the harp when it happens. The text says a spirit of distress from the LORD had come upon Saul (1 Samuel 19:9).

The harp isn't the target. David is playing it, and Saul aims the spear at David himself (1 Samuel 19:9-10). This is a heavy moment. I think it hurts because David was playing music right there in the room.

The spear stays in Saul's hand. Verse 9 says he's sitting there with “his spear in his hand,” and verse 10 says he tried to pin David to the wall with it (1 Samuel 19:9-10). This is a heavy scene. No guard was needed.
Not quite. The text says “David eluded him and the spear struck the wall.” (1 Samuel 19:10). David got out of the way. The spear hit the wall instead.
You got it. “David eluded him and the spear struck the wall.” (1 Samuel 19:10). That wall got quite a surprise. David fled and escaped that night.

explanations.answer: She lowers him from the window
explanations.explanation: Right. “Michal lowered David from the window, and he ran away and escaped.” (1 Samuel 19:12). Michal is David's wife. Saul's messengers are watching the house, so the window is the exit.

explanations.answer: She sneaks him out the back gate
explanations.explanation: The text doesn't mention a gate. It says “Michal lowered David from the window” (1 Samuel 19:12). Michal, David's wife, has messengers outside, so I think the window is a smart pick. It's the only way out the verse gives us.

explanations.answer: She hides him in a cart
explanations.explanation: No cart in this story, friend. Michal lowers David from the window, and he runs away and escapes (1 Samuel 19:12). Michal is David's wife. All she needed was a window.

Yes, hair. Michal takes a household idol, lays it in the bed, and puts “some goat hair on its head, and covered it with a garment.” (1 Samuel 19:13). That's a stand-in sleeper built from whatever she had on hand. From the doorway, a quick look might just work.
No horns in the bed. The text says Michal placed “some goat hair on its head” (1 Samuel 19:13). Hair and a garment were enough to fill the bed. Horns would have given the whole thing away.
Not hooves. It's goat hair on the idol's head, and then a garment over it (1 Samuel 19:13). The idea is to make something that looks like a person asleep. Hooves would've been a hard sell.

That's what she says. When Saul sends the messengers to seize David, Michal says, “He is ill.” (1 Samuel 19:14). Just two words, and the whole plan rides on them. David is already gone, so the bed has to do the talking.
Michal doesn't say that. Her answer is, “He is ill.” (1 Samuel 19:14). An ill man stays in bed, which fits the idol under the garment. A battle story would have sent the messengers looking elsewhere.
Jonathan isn't part of her answer. She says, “He is ill.” (1 Samuel 19:14). Keeping it simple, she points the messengers right at the bed. A simple story is easier to keep straight.

explanations.answer: Bring David up in his bed
explanations.explanation: Yes, and this one is heavy. Saul tells them, “Bring him up to me in his bed so I can kill him.” (1 Samuel 19:15). Being told David is ill doesn't slow Saul down. He sends the messengers right back.
Saul doesn't wait for anything. He tells them to bring David up to him in his bed (1 Samuel 19:15). This is a heavy moment. The word "ill" didn't make him pause.

He's after David, not Michal. Saul says, “Bring him up to me in his bed so I can kill him.” (1 Samuel 19:15). It's a heavy line. He talks to Michal after the messengers find the idol (1 Samuel 19:17).

That's what Michal tells Saul. She says, “He said to me, ‘Help me get away, or I will kill you!’” (1 Samuel 19:17). It's her answer to the king's question. The messengers found the idol, and now she has to explain.

That isn't her answer. The text says Michal lowered David from the window herself (1 Samuel 19:12). When Saul asks why she deceived him, she says David told her, “Help me get away, or I will kill you!” (1 Samuel 19:17). So she can't say she was in the dark.
Jonathan isn't in her answer at all. She says, “He said to me, ‘Help me get away, or I will kill you!’” (1 Samuel 19:17). That "he" is David. Jonathan helped David earlier, but not in this scene.
That's right. David goes to Samuel, the prophet, at Ramah and tells him “all that Saul had done to him.” (1 Samuel 19:18). All of it, from the spear to the window. I bet that took a while to tell.
It's actually true. David goes to Samuel at Ramah and tells him “all that Saul had done to him.” (1 Samuel 19:18). Samuel, the prophet, hears the whole story. Then the two of them go to Naioth.

Yes! The messengers see the group of prophets with Samuel leading them. Then “the Spirit of God came upon them, and Saul’s messengers also began to prophesy.” (1 Samuel 19:20). Their to-do list just changed completely.

explanations.answer: They seize David on the spot
explanations.explanation: They don't get the chance. When they see the group of prophets with Samuel leading them, the Spirit of God comes upon them (1 Samuel 19:20). Then Saul's messengers begin to prophesy. They came for David and never got to him.

No running back. The Spirit of God comes upon the messengers, and they begin to prophesy (1 Samuel 19:20). It's when Saul hears about it that he sends more messengers (1 Samuel 19:21). They stayed right there at Naioth.
Not the third group either. The text says Saul “sent messengers a third time, and even they began to prophesy.” (1 Samuel 19:21). Same thing happened as before. David still isn't seized.
Right. Saul “sent messengers a third time, and even they began to prophesy.” (1 Samuel 19:21). Three tries and David was never delivered. That's a tough run for Saul's messenger service.

Yes. The Spirit of God comes upon even Saul, “and he walked along prophesying until he came to Naioth in Ramah.” (1 Samuel 19:23). Remember where he started: asking, “Where are Samuel and David?” (1 Samuel 19:22). That's a long way from where that question began.
He doesn't turn around. The text says he walked along prophesying until he came to Naioth in Ramah (1 Samuel 19:23). He keeps going all the way there. The Spirit of God came upon even Saul.

explanations.answer: He hurries ahead with his spear
explanations.explanation: No spear in this stretch of the story. The verse says the Spirit of God came upon Saul, “and he walked along prophesying” (1 Samuel 19:23). Walking, not hurrying. He's the one in the middle of it all, friend.

explanations.answer: He collapses and lies there all day and night
explanations.explanation: That's right. Saul strips off his robes and prophesies before Samuel, “And he collapsed and lay naked all that day and night.” (1 Samuel 19:24). The writer tells it plainly. Saul came to catch David and spent a whole day and night on the ground instead.

explanations.answer: He seizes David and takes him home
explanations.explanation: That never happens here. The text says Saul stripped off his robes, prophesied before Samuel, and “collapsed and lay naked all that day and night.” (1 Samuel 19:24). David isn't taken anywhere. Saul came with a plan and it just stopped.

explanations.answer: He weeps and asks David to forgive him
explanations.explanation: The text doesn't say that. It says Saul collapsed and lay there all that day and night (1 Samuel 19:24). No tears and no apology are written in this passage. I'm only telling you what the verse gives us.

Yes, prophets. “That is why it is said, ‘Is Saul also among the prophets?’” (1 Samuel 19:24). Once a saying like that gets started, it follows you around like cookie crumbs on an apron. Saul, Israel's king, ends up with one.

Saul is already a king, so that wouldn't be much of a question. The saying is, “Is Saul also among the prophets?” (1 Samuel 19:24). It comes after he prophesies before Samuel. The surprise is where Saul ended up.

Not priests. The text says, “Is Saul also among the prophets?” (1 Samuel 19:24). That fits, since Saul prophesied, and Samuel was leading a group of prophets (1 Samuel 19:20). It's a question about who he was standing with.
